content: Calcium carbonate is an antacid that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of heartburn, sour stomach, acid indigestion, and upset stomach associated with these symptoms. Common side effects include constipation, flatulence, and abdominal bloating. For adults, calcium carbonate is indicated for the prevention and treatment of calcium deficiency. The recommended daily allowance (RDA) for individuals aged 19 to 50 years is 1000 mg of elemental calcium per day, divided into doses of 500 mg or less, with a maximum daily intake of 2500 mg. For men aged 51 to 70 years, the RDA remains 1000 mg per day, with a maximum of 2000 mg daily. For women aged 51 to 70 years, the RDA increases to 1200 mg per day, with a maximum of 2000 mg daily. For individuals over 70 years of age, the RDA is 1200 mg per day, with a maximum of 2000 mg daily. In pediatric populations, calcium carbonate is also used for the prevention and treatment of calcium deficiency. The RDA varies by age group: For infants aged 0 to 6 months, the RDA is 200 mg per day, with a maximum of 1000 mg daily. For infants aged 6 to 12 months, the RDA is 260 mg per day, with a maximum of 1500 mg daily. For children aged 1 to 3 years, the RDA is 700 mg per day, with a maximum of 2500 mg daily. For children aged 4 to 8 years, the RDA is 1000 mg per day, with a maximum of 2500 mg daily. For children aged 9 to 13 years, the RDA is 1300 mg per day, with a maximum of 3000 mg daily. For adolescents aged 14 to 18 years, the RDA is 1300 mg per day, with a maximum of 3000 mg daily. Off-label uses of calcium carbonate include the treatment of chemical burns caused by hydrofluoric acid, prevention of bone fractures, management of chronic hypocalcemia, and treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis. It is also used for heartburn relief. Calcium carbonate should be used with caution in individuals with kidney stones or those on a calcium-restricted diet. Patients taking prescription medications should consult a healthcare provider before using calcium carbonate, as antacids may interact with certain drugs. When using this product, do not exceed 10 tablets in 24 hours or use the maximum dosage for more than two weeks. Keep this medication out of reach of children. Serious adverse effects associated with calcium carbonate include myocardial infarction, urolithiasis, prostate cancer, and milk-alkali syndrome. Common gastrointestinal side effects include constipation, flatulence, and abdominal bloating. There is limited information regarding the use of calcium carbonate during pregnancy, labor and delivery, or breastfeeding. Similarly, there is no specific FDA guidance on its use in pediatric, geriatric, gender-specific, racial, renal-impaired, hepatic-impaired, or immunocompromised populations. Calcium carbonate is administered orally. There is limited information on monitoring requirements, IV compatibility, overdose management, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology. In case of suspected overdose, contact the National Poison Help hotline immediately. Calcium carbonate should be stored at a temperature of 20–25°C (68–77°F). There is no established interaction between calcium carbonate and alcohol, but patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding potential effects.
